The Decay of Urban Spaces

By: Julian Sun | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The influx of homeless people into the suburbs is leading to the urban decay of public spaces. How does one balance compassion for the homeless a with the needs of communities that feel under existent

Unique Selling Point:
Carte Blanche grapples with the impact of homelessness on public spaces, a complex problem with no obvious and easy solutions

Summary:
A failing economy is driving more and more people into poverty leading to an influx of desperate people to middle-class suburbs in search of opportunity. The result is that residential streets, urban parks and other public spaces are becoming overrun by a mixture of homeless people, substance abusers and illegal immigrants.

The problem is being exacerbated by the failure of the authorities to enforce by-laws hastening the degradation of these important public spaces. People can be found loitering illegally on sidewalks, sleeping in front of shops and inside city parks themselves. In the worst cases, abandoned buildings are hijacked and transformed into squalid informal settlements that threaten the safety of residents, the environment and the fiscal sustainability of small businesses - that are so vital to the South African economy.

How does one balance compassion for the homeless a with the needs of communities that feel under existential threat?

Thabiso Kibe

The Decay of Public Spaces Script v4
Scene Setter
Anthony: [00:00:44] It was around 7 p.m. on a Saturday evening.
Anthony: [00:00:53] We heard a couple of gunshots.
Anthony: [00:01:00] So I ran out to find out what was happening
Anthony: [00:01:10] I could see people hunched over on the pathway here. So I approached them, and that's when I noticed, Marcel, who was shot.

Visuals: Exterior Day: Establishing Shot: Delta Park from Drone

VOICE OVER: Delta is one of the largest and most popular City Parks in Johannesburg but its peace and tranquility was shattered last month when a local resident was attacked while walking his dogs. Eyewitness Anthony Burton was one of the first on the scene.
Anthony: [00:01:39] It appeared to be a robbery gone bad
Anthony: [00:01:55] You know, the dog was unfortunately shot and killed as well and Marcel had some very near, near fatal wounds on him.

Anthony: [00:04:17] And this was quite, quite personal because someone got really hurt. And it happened on our doorstep

VOICE OVER: The man was rushed to hospital and is recovering after the attack but his assailants remain at large.

Dip to Black

VOICE OVER: Attacks like this have caused people to fear using public spaces like Delta Park which is part of a 37km green belt with the Braamfontein Spruit as its spine. It flows through some of Johannesburg’s most affluent Northern Suburbs.

With unemployment at crisis levels, this green belt is being increasingly used as a last refuge for the desperate and the homeless. With decades of experience in Private Security, Andre Aiton is deeply concerned.

Andre: [00:12:03] I'm very worried about crime increasing in the Delta. It's a long channel. It stretches from Albert's Farm right the way through to the suburbs of Sandton. We've seen that there's been a murder in a very close proximity very recently.
Andre: [00:14:07] I believe it's going to get worse, unfortunately, with the unemployment that we have at the moment and they have nowhere to go.
V/O: In the wake of the Delta Park shooting, a joint operation between the SAPS and several private security companies was launched in the early hours of the morning. With the help of a thermal drone, the police were able to pick up the heat signatures of people sleeping illegally in the park.

Andre: There was roughly 15 individuals that were taken in for profiling to the local police station. We did manage to find a plastic firearm or a gas gun, knives, multiple knobkerries, and stuff like that.
Anthony: [00:06:24] it is a concern from the community that, yes, an increase in vagrants in the park is leading to an increase of crime in the area.
Drone Footage of the Braamfontein Spruit showing litter, recycling, and people living in the Spruit

V/O: A bird’s eye view of the Spruit reveals the scale of the problem. Not only are there people living along its banks but they also pollute the stream, leading to conflict with residents of suburbs like Victory Park that lie adjacent to it. Reyahna Satar moved here from Lenasia, in search of a better life.
Reyhana: [00:01:10] The dream was to live and have a lifestyle. Being able to jog, being able to cycle within the parks. And that's the reason we moved here.
V/O: But that dream has become a nightmare

Reyhana: [00:02:36] Look, I think the big thing is crime increased. We've had eight incidents in our house.

Mac: [00:02:44] Eight here?

Reyhana: [00:21:15] The most recent incident happened on the 27th of December. We were thankfully sleeping. But anything could have happened. We could have interrupted them... My daughters could have interrupted them during the robbery. And then what?

Montage of homelessness and vagrancy on the streets of Johannesburg

V/O: Homelessness is a crisis playing out in towns and cities all over South Africa. These days it’s common to see people living in parks or loitering outside local businesses. Substance abuse is a major issue and some are often drunk and disorderly.

Macfarlane Link: I’ve always wanted to see what the streets of Joburg are like at night so we’re going to go out with a private security company to see what happens, especially with the vagrants, when the sun sets.

A sequence of a night patrol that ends with a sound byte of Mac talking to a drunk man outside a shopfront.

Mac: So is this where you sleep?

Homeless: Yes this is where I sleep, it’s my place.

Mac: So there’s no one who can take it from you?

Homeless: No, I’m going to beat them!

V/O: The are over 15000 homeless in Johannesburg. It’s illegal to sleep on the streets but the sheer volume of people has left the JMPD overwhelmed and unable to enforce by-laws. Even though there are city shelters many homeless people refuse to use them.
Reyhana: [00:10:49] There is no willingness to actually go to shelters because then you cannot follow. You can cannot drink. So you have to follow rules. So we are sitting at an impasse with respect to that.
V/O: Instead they choose to live rough on the streets of suburbs like Linden. Charitable feeding schemes provide food, but is this actually helping?

Clement: [00:11:37] We have like five churches, four churches that are feeding schemes, but outside of Linden. Not really. This is why everybody flocks to Linden the whole time. Because not just that Linden is very safe area when it comes to concentration of security. The people of Linden, believe it or not, they are good-hearted people. Yeah, they do help. They feed us. And this is why most people come here because of food.

Mac: [00:23:55] What are your thoughts around feeding schemes?

Reyhana: [00:24:03] Look, I think it's a necessary, immediate thing. There is an issue with people not obviously having food. So we are in the process of talking to the NGOs. There's no incentive for people to improve their condition and their life if you giving handouts.

V/O: The guarantee of safety and a daily meal draws homeless people to Linden bringing them into direct conflict with residents who feel these soup kitchens are enabling the problem. Small business owners are up in arms, as they must constantly clean their shopfronts, protect customers from harassment and deal with petty break-ins. It’s a complex problem that pits compassion for the homeless against the need to protect businesses and livelihoods in suburban business districts.

Andre: [00:20:59] if we don't start to all get together and make a difference, nothing's going to change but it's going to take more and that's why I'm urging residents to come out, get involved, and make a difference.

V/O: One NPO chipping away at the problem is “Let’s Work”. Since 2017 they’ve been helping the unemployed by providing daily work to try and get them back on their feet. Volunteers like Thabiso KIbe earn a small stipend cleaning public spaces like the Spruit.

Q: How did you end up going there? Were you unemployed?
A: I was working then lost my job, I was fired then lived on the streets.

Thabiso: We used to go stay in parks, camping in parks and we’d go hustle for work

Thabiso: It’s not nice there, we’d eat in tins, we even cook in them, we would drink from water on the ground because even when when we go to the garages they wouldn’t allow us in because we’re homeless.

Q: Because you lived in parks and there were houses around, how did the community treat you?
A: They treated us badly, some would call the cops to remove us

Segway to Parkhurst

V/O: And while the greenbelt continues grappling with this complex issue, in the nearby suburb of Parkhurst it's become even more acute. That’s because the abandoned bowling club property has become home to dozens if not hundreds of people.




MAC LINK: This is the Parkhurst Bowling Club, a once-thriving location that has now been reduced to squalor. Surrounded by waste and rubbish, but for some people this is “home” if you can call it that.

Mac explores the bowling club, we see him walking through the exterior, meeting some of the people who live there.

MAC LINK: It’s quite weird, it’s almost like a tale of two cities right? You’ve got a leafy suburb on your right-hand side, Victory Park and you’ve got this like almost informal settlement that is now starting to mushroom here.

Drone shots of Parkhurst Bowling Club adjacent to the affluent suburb of Parkhurst

V/O: The people who live in the bowling club are predominantly waste pickers drawn to Parkhurst by a controversial sorting site across the road. Mike Rosholt represents the residents and business owners association.

Mike: [00:09:39] What we've seen is that over the years, the site is too small and so those activities have moved across the road to the bowling club.

Mike: [00:04:18] Unfortunately, in the last couple of years, particularly the last year, we've gone from 30 or 40 to about 200 people living on site.

Mike: [00:02:58] There's a shebeen. There are drugs available to you at any time of the day. We know there's prostitution. We've had human trafficking issues there. We've had three dead bodies on site. One of them supposedly a murder.

V/O: Many local businesses and residents see this burgeoning informal settlement as a threat to their livelihoods and assets.

Cutaways of the walk and talk through the suburbs of Parkhurst, along with shots of houses and shops

Mike Rosholt (walk and talk): [00:04:25] The landlords can't afford and the traders can't afford, and frankly, the residents can't afford to have this high street go like some of the other high streets around Johannesburg.

Mike: [00:16:40] Because ultimately, if Parkhurst fails, those jobs go away. The value of the properties go down. None of us are able to pay our rates in that case. And so the problem will only spiral. [00:16:55][14.5]

Mike: [00:16:15] If the problem drags on on its current trajectory, we're going to have a proper informal settlement. This will be from 200 to upwards of 1000 people. It's a fairly large site at over eight hectares, which is obviously a huge concern [00:16:27][11.8

V/O: It’s a worst-case scenario that has already come to pass in the suburb of Hurlingham which is the site of an informal settlement of more than 1000 people. What’s clear is that homelessness is a complex and nuanced issue with no easy solutions.

Reyhana: [00:10:18] They try to sort of peg the narrative as residents against homeless people. But it's not right. We also trying to find an empathetic solution where everybody benefits from the situation. And we don't think the current situation is sustainable. The reclaimers don't get access to contracts. They're not paid fair wage. They’re forced to live in undignified conditions, which doesn't make them richer. It keeps them poorer.

V/O: And yet, for all the criticism of informal settlements, they remain the closest thing to home people like Thabiso will ever know. Thanks to the efforts of Let’s Work, he now has a roof over his head."

End with the close-up portrait of Thabiso smiling outside his home


PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: In Johannesburg, residential streets, and parks are becoming overrun by homeless people, substance abusers, and undocumented immigrants.

UPSOUND: Reyhana: [00:02:36] Look, I think the big thing is crime increased. We've had eight incidents in our house.

Mac: [00:02:44] Eight here?

VO: Ratepayers are concerned, but it’s a problem throughout the country.


PROMO 2
V/O: Rising unemployment is forcing more and more people to seek refuge in city parks and street corners in Johannesburg

Clement: They feed us. And this is why most people come here because of food.

VO: But can the City balance compassion for the homeless with the needs of its ratepayers?



PROMO 3

VO: In Johannesburg, residential streets, and parks are becoming overrun homeless people, illegal immigrants and opportunistic criminals.

Mike: [00:02:14] We have a lot of litter, waste being sorted in sites where it shouldn't be. We've got environmental degradation along our green spaces and a large uptick in crime generally.

VO: Ratepayers are fed-up, but there are no easy answers.

Thabiso: We used to go stay in parks, camping in parks and we’d go hustle for work Thabiso: It’s not nice there, we’d eat in tins, we even cook in them, we would drink from water on the ground because even when when we go to the garages they wouldn’t allow us in because we’re homeless. Q: Because you lived in parks and there were houses around, how did the community treat you? A: They treated us badly, some would call the cops to remove us Segway to Parkhurst V/O: And while the greenbelt continues grappling with this complex issue, in the nearby suburb of Parkhurst it's become even more acute. That’s because the abandoned bowling club property has become home to dozens if not hundreds of people. MAC LINK: This is the Parkhurst Bowling Club, a once-thriving location that has now been reduced to squalor. Surrounded by waste and rubbish, but for some people this is “home” if you can call it that. Mac explores the bowling club, we see him walking through the exterior, meeting some of the people who live there. MAC LINK: It’s quite weird, it’s almost like a tale of two cities right? You’ve got a leafy suburb on your right-hand side, Victory Park and you’ve got this like almost informal settlement that is now starting to mushroom here. Drone shots of Parkhurst Bowling Club adjacent to the affluent suburb of Parkhurst V/O: The people who live in the bowling club are predominantly waste pickers drawn to Parkhurst by a controversial sorting site across the road. Mike Rosholt represents the residents and business owners association. Mike: [00:09:39] What we've seen is that over the years, the site is too small and so those activities have moved across the road to the bowling club. Mike: [00:04:18] Unfortunately, in the last couple of years, particularly the last year, we've gone from 30 or 40 to about 200 people living on site. Mike: [00:02:58] There's a shebeen. There are drugs available to you at any time of the day. We know there's prostitution. We've had human trafficking issues there. We've had three dead bodies on site. One of them supposedly a murder. V/O: Many local businesses and residents see this burgeoning informal settlement as a threat to their livelihoods and assets. Cutaways of the walk and talk through the suburbs of Parkhurst, along with shots of houses and shops Mike Rosholt (walk and talk): [00:04:25] The landlords can't afford and the traders can't afford, and frankly, the residents can't afford to have this high street go like some of the other high streets around Johannesburg. Mike: [00:16:40] Because ultimately, if Parkhurst fails, those jobs go away. The value of the properties go down. None of us are able to pay our rates in that case. And so the problem will only spiral. [00:16:55][14.5] Mike: [00:16:15] If the problem drags on on its current trajectory, we're going to have a proper informal settlement. This will be from 200 to upwards of 1000 people. It's a fairly large site at over eight hectares, which is obviously a huge concern [00:16:27][11.8 V/O: It’s a worst-case scenario that has already come to pass in the suburb of Hurlingham which is the site of an informal settlement of more than 1000 people. What’s clear is that homelessness is a complex and nuanced issue with no easy solutions. Reyhana: [00:10:18] They try to sort of peg the narrative as residents against homeless people. But it's not right. We also trying to find an empathetic solution where everybody benefits from the situation. And we don't think the current situation is sustainable. The reclaimers don't get access to contracts. They're not paid fair wage. They’re forced to live in undignified conditions, which doesn't make them richer. It keeps them poorer. V/O: And yet, for all the criticism of informal settlements, they remain the closest thing to home people like Thabiso will ever know. metadata.Unique Selling Point: Carte Blanche grapples with the impact of homelessness on public spaces, a complex problem with no obvious and easy solutions
metadata.Summary: A failing economy is driving more and more people into poverty leading to an influx of desperate people to middle-class suburbs in search of opportunity. The result is that residential streets, urban parks and other public spaces are becoming overrun by a mixture of homeless people, substance abusers and illegal immigrants. The problem is being exacerbated by the failure of the authorities to enforce by-laws hastening the degradation of these important public spaces. People can be found loitering illegally on sidewalks, sleeping in front of shops and inside city parks themselves. In the worst cases, abandoned buildings are hijacked and transformed into squalid informal settlements that threaten the safety of residents, the environment and the fiscal sustainability of small businesses - that are so vital to the South African economy. How does one balance compassion for the homeless a with the needs of communities that feel under existential threat?
